title: Too dark, or the good kind of dark?
author: Wonderful_Ad4736
selftext:
I am currently playing with lights, particles and shadows to make it more polished. Do you think it is too dark, considering the robot is in the basement of an office building? What would you recommend to make the game look better (apart from the character, which will be replaced later)?   
  
*Context: This is an entry-level of my game, where you get to know the character who you just saw for the first time through a camera (player is camera operator in charge of a robot)*

comments.author: Specific_Ordinary499
comments.body:
If players find the game too dark they will up the brightness anyways.  
Game looks good though! Loving the CRT esthetic, those rolling scanlines.

replies.author: Wonderful_Ad4736
replies.body: True. I need to add a brightness slider to settings once I get to that stage

comments.author: bingewavecinema
comments.body: It depends on the theme and if it affects playablity. You have to run playtests and see

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body: The lighting pass sells it, yes. You do put a large burden on your level authoring to ensure that the lighting can carry the scene, but yes. I'd just make sure that your palette isn't going to get too old after 8 hours of playing and that you have ways to make it feel fresh considering the monochrome. But otherwise yes.

replies.author: Wonderful_Ad4736
replies.body: I am planning more “biomes” as the robot goes up the levels, this will be one of the darkest ones I imagine

comments.author: GulbrandrGameStudios
comments.body: Game design advice. If it seems dark to you, it’s dark.

comments.author: IsThisASnakeInMyBoot
comments.body: If it's supposed to be a horror game, the first option. Anything else, I would probably say halfway between the 2

replies.author: Wonderful_Ad4736
replies.body: Thanks, from other comments I need to bump the light up a bit. The gify makes things even worse but that is not an excuse

replies.author: IsThisASnakeInMyBoot
replies.body: Honestly the second one seems too bright if you want a dimly lit basement. Looks closer to the light level you'd see in the deep dark in minecraft, which has like magical lighting, and the first one looks closer to an unlit cave that's why I think a halfway point would be a better fit

replies.author: Wonderful_Ad4736
replies.body: The first one is no light, that one is no-go. The second you are right, feels too magical. Thanks!

comments.author: kryptondog
comments.body:
I love the aesthetics of the character and the levels! Do you mind me asking how you're building assets?

To answer your question from my POV: I think it depends on whether darkness is an active component of the gameplay loop. I'm working on a dungeon crawler with a somewhat similar look and feel - many of the rooms will be oppressively dark with just a few light sources, so that you only see enemies when you aggro them. There's a lot more to it, but I won't highjack your thread haha - mainly mentioning to say that if you foresee using darkness in a similar manner, I think it could work, so long as it's done with intentionality and doesn't collide with your other gameplay mechanics.

Even if that's not the case though, I think the darkness would make sense for certain environments (like a basement as you mentioned), though I'd definitely consider using it sparingly for better effect - it'd be a great contrast for brighter areas imo.

(Not a real game designer at all, just someone who's been thinking about stuff like this way too much with my own game haha - just my two cents!)

replies.author: Wonderful_Ad4736
replies.body:
Thank you.

It is combination of 
1. hand made
2. claude drawn (have a simple rendering pipeline that allows agents to draw new assets in specified pixel grid so it feels on brand)
3. Also experimenting with just free 3D models rendered at specific angle into a 2D sprite with blender cli and then pixelated into the same grid as other assets. (All the tables, chairs are done with this)

comments.author: AlarakReigns
comments.body: Without lighting it doesnt make sense for our brains to have a character that is shining in a dark room an orange color. Character likely needs a light source unless its part of direction to have things appear brighter than their environment purposefully.

replies.author: Wonderful_Ad4736
replies.body: There is a lightsource right in the very cente (on the 2nd version). What I am struggling with in this camera is how to show it. If I put some lightbar stripe it looks odd but without I have the issue you mention that it is unclear there is one

replies.author: AlarakReigns
replies.body:
If you are talking about how to show the source of the light is emnating light, typically the object needs to show something that it looks "on". If we look at something like Diablo, shrines that have a glow effect have a candle or the runewords glow, but if you interact with it they turn off ans the candlelight dissipates then turns off the light source. 

Diablo 1 has my favorite lighting in a video game, because it accomplishes a lot using dithering techniques, but it is using 3d isometric assets for a 2d playing field except for the floor tiles. The source code of D1 is open source and if you feed it to your ai it might understand something it didnt before even if that lighting isnt part of your main vision.  Diablo 1 pre renders and bakes the models that were 3d and gives its own natural lighting for the models using its dithering lighting.

comments.author: HoloArcade
comments.body: add a slider in the game settings and let user adjust between a min/max you pre-define, this way if there is an accessibility reason or the user just prefers it a bit differently then they can adjust it, and by default it uses what you deam is best
